body:
From conventional breeding to genetic engineering

Conventional plant breeding combines genetic variation through crossing and selects plants with useful traits. Marker-assisted selection makes this selection more precise by identifying DNA markers associated with desired traits.

Genetic engineering directly alters the genetic material of an organism using molecular techniques. The change may involve adding, removing or modifying DNA. A genetically modified organism (GMO) is an organism whose genetic material has been deliberately changed through genetic engineering.

A transgenic crop contains genetic material introduced from another organism. Transgenesis is one form of genetic modification, but the broad term genetic modification is not limited to inserting genes from unrelated species.

Bt cotton: a major Indian example

Bt cotton contains selected genes originally obtained from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis. These genes enable the plant to produce proteins that are toxic to certain susceptible insect pests, especially targeted bollworms.

The insecticidal proteins are commonly called Cry proteins, after the genes that encode them. Specific Cry proteins act against particular insect groups. In susceptible insect larvae, the appropriate toxin becomes active in the gut, binds to suitable targets and damages gut cells, leading to the insect's death.

Bt cotton is therefore an example of insect-resistant genetic modification. It should not be described as a crop resistant to every insect pest, every disease or every environmental stress. Pest resistance can also develop over time, making appropriate resistance management important.

India approved Bt cotton for commercial cultivation in 2002. A Government of India reply dated 6 August 2024 identified Bt cotton as the country's only GM crop approved for commercial cultivation at that time. Gujarat is one of India's important cotton-growing states, making Bt cotton a direct agricultural example relevant to the state.

Genome editing

Genome editing makes targeted changes at selected locations in an organism's DNA. CRISPR-Cas is a widely known genome-editing technology. Its important conceptual feature is the ability to direct a change to a chosen genetic location.

Genome editing can alter an organism's existing genetic material without permanently adding DNA from another species. However, genome editing can also be used in applications involving inserted DNA. Therefore, the statement that every genome-edited organism is free of foreign DNA is incorrect.

MethodWhat it principally doesDoes it inherently introduce foreign DNA?
Conventional breedingCrosses and selects plantsNo
Marker-assisted selectionUses DNA markers to select offspringNo
Transgenic modificationIntroduces genetic material from another organismYes, by definition
Genome editingMakes targeted DNA changesNot necessarily

India's genome-edited rice varieties

On 4 May 2025, the Indian Council of Agricultural Research announced the development of 2 genome-edited rice varieties:

  • DRR Rice 100 (Kamla): developed by ICAR-Indian Institute of Rice Research, Hyderabad, using Samba Mahsuri as the starting variety.
  • Pusa DST Rice 1: developed by ICAR-Indian Agricultural Research Institute, New Delhi, using MTU 1010 as the starting variety.

ICAR described these as products of CRISPR-Cas-based editing without introduced foreign DNA. Their announcement as developed varieties must not be confused with the separate commercial approval history of transgenic Bt cotton. Development, regulatory clearance, seed availability and widespread cultivation are distinct stages.

Why assessment remains important

A desired genetic change does not automatically guarantee improved performance in every environment. A crop must be evaluated for the intended trait and relevant agricultural, food, feed or environmental considerations. The kind of assessment depends on the product and the applicable regulatory framework.

Prelims focus

  • Bt stands for Bacillus thuringiensis; Cry proteins provide resistance against particular susceptible insects.
  • Bt cotton received India's commercial cultivation approval in 2002.
  • A Government reply dated 6 August 2024 identified Bt cotton as the only commercially approved GM crop at that time.
  • Genome editing can change existing DNA without introducing foreign DNA.
  • ICAR announced DRR Rice 100 (Kamla) and Pusa DST Rice 1 on 4 May 2025.
  • Trap: Genome-edited rice development and transgenic Bt cotton approval are not equivalent regulatory events.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, ch. 12, 'Biotechnology and Its Applications', §12.1; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, ch. 11, 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', §§11.1–11.3; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, 'Cultivation of Genetically Modified Crops', 6 August 2024; Indian Council of Agricultural Research, 'Two Genome-Edited Rice Varieties Developed in India', 4 April 2025, consulted 13 November 2026.]

title: Genetically Modified Crops and Genome-Edited Crops

body:
What is synthetic biology?

Synthetic biology is a field that applies scientific and engineering ideas to design, construct or redesign biological components and systems for useful functions. It draws on genetics, molecular biology, biotechnology and the study of how biological processes are regulated.

Traditional biotechnology often uses an organism's existing ability, such as yeast fermentation. Genetic engineering may alter a specific gene or introduce a selected genetic characteristic. Synthetic biology frequently goes further by combining biological components so that a cell performs a planned function, responds to a chosen signal or produces a useful substance.

These categories overlap. A synthetic-biology system may use genetic engineering, but not every genetically modified organism is an example of a deliberately designed synthetic biological system.

What are engineered biological systems?

An engineered biological system is a biological arrangement intentionally modified or organised to perform a particular function. The system may be a microorganism, a group of cells or a set of interacting biological components.

Useful functions include producing a chemical, detecting a substance or responding to an environmental condition. An engineered organism remains a living biological system with limitations. Its behaviour can depend on the environment, nutrient availability, interactions among genes and other biological conditions.

Genes, gene expression and regulation

Genes contain information used to produce functional RNA molecules or proteins. Gene expression is the process by which this information contributes to a functional product. The activity of genes is controlled by regulatory mechanisms.

Cells do not express every gene at the same level all the time. Some genes become more active or less active in response to environmental signals. Synthetic biology can make use of these regulatory relationships to develop useful biological responses.

Gene circuits

A gene circuit is a set of interacting genetic and regulatory components that produces a particular pattern of gene activity or biological response. Its behaviour can be understood through the relationship between an input signal, regulation of gene expression and an output.

Consider a conceptual microbial sensing system. The presence of a particular environmental substance serves as an input. A suitable regulatory system responds to that input and changes the activity of a gene. The resulting output might be a detectable signal or the production of a specified biological substance.

A gene circuit does not have to operate as a simple permanent switch. Biological regulation may be temporary and conditional. The important prelims-level principle is that interactions among genetic components can produce a coordinated response.

Applications of synthetic biology

Application areaPossible engineered functionPurpose
Industrial productionMicroorganisms produce selected chemicalsManufacturing useful substances
Environmental monitoringBiological systems respond to selected substancesDetecting relevant environmental signals
Environmental treatmentEngineered organisms perform useful transformationsSupporting pollution treatment
AgricultureBiological functions are modified for useful traitsImproving agricultural applications

For example, microorganisms may be engineered to produce a valuable chemical rather than relying on its extraction from a natural source. In another application, a biological sensing system may indicate the presence of a selected environmental contaminant.

Why synthetic biology requires careful evaluation

A designed biological function may behave differently under different conditions. A microorganism that performs usefully in a controlled production facility may not behave identically in an open environment. Important considerations include stability of the desired function, possible interactions with other organisms, unintended effects and suitable containment.

Thus, the ability to design a biological function does not establish that an engineered organism is safe for unrestricted environmental release. The intended use and exposure conditions must be considered separately.

Prelims focus

  • Synthetic biology involves designing or redesigning biological functions.
  • Gene expression produces functional RNA or protein products from genetic information.
  • A gene circuit links interacting genetic components to a coordinated biological response.
  • Inputs can alter gene regulation and thereby change biological outputs.
  • Synthetic-biology applications include manufacturing, sensing and environmental biotechnology.
  • Trap: All synthetic-biology systems are not simply conventional fermentation systems, and not every genetic modification is necessarily synthetic biology.

[Sources: National Human Genome Research Institute, 'Synthetic Biology', sections on definition, applications and distinction from genome editing, consulted 13 November 2026; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, ch. 11, 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', §11.1; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, ch. 6, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', sections on gene expression and regulation.]

pictures.alt: An environmental input alters gene expression, producing a detectable signal or specified substance; the response can depend on biological conditions.
pictures.caption: A gene circuit connects an input signal with a regulated biological output.

title: Synthetic Biology and Gene Circuits

body:
Why biotechnology needs governance

Biotechnology can improve agriculture, manufacturing and environmental management, but biological systems can also produce unintended effects. Governance provides rules and institutions for evaluating risks, controlling particular activities and supporting responsible applications.

Two important terms must be distinguished:

  • Biosafety concerns the prevention of accidental harm to people, animals, plants and the environment from biological agents, organisms and biotechnology activities.
  • Biosecurity concerns measures to prevent unauthorised access, deliberate misuse, theft or intentional harmful use of biological materials and related capabilities.

The terms are related but not identical. An accidental release from a facility primarily raises a biosafety concern. Deliberate misuse or unauthorised access raises a biosecurity concern. Some safeguards contribute to both.

Contained use and environmental release

Contained use involves biological activities undertaken with appropriate physical or operational barriers intended to limit exposure and escape. An enclosed industrial production system is conceptually different from deliberate release of an organism into the environment.

Environmental release can create opportunities for an organism to interact with crops, wild species, soil organisms and other components of ecosystems. Consequently, the environmental implications of an engineered organism require assessment relevant to the intended release.

India's regulatory framework

The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 provides an important statutory basis for India's framework concerning genetically engineered organisms and certain hazardous microorganisms.

The 1989 Rules, formally concerning the manufacture, use, import, export and storage of hazardous microorganisms, genetically engineered organisms or cells, establish an important regulatory framework under this Act.

BodyFull namePrincipal role
IBSCInstitutional Biosafety CommitteeInstitution-level biosafety oversight of relevant activities
RCGMReview Committee on Genetic ManipulationReview and oversight of relevant genetic-manipulation research under DBT
GEACGenetic Engineering Appraisal CommitteeAppraisal of specified large-scale activities and environmental release proposals

The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) functions under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. Its responsibilities include appraisal of proposals for environmental release of genetically engineered organisms, including relevant experimental field trials.

The committee was formerly called the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee. The name was changed to Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee by a notification dated 16 July 2010, effective from 22 July 2010. Older books may retain the former name, but the current institutional expansion is Appraisal.

India's 2022 provisions for genome-edited plants

On 30 March 2022, the central government issued an exemption concerning specified categories of genome-edited plants. SDN means site-directed nuclease; SDN-1 editing uses no DNA repair template, while SDN-2 uses one to make specific small changes. Under the stated conditions, SDN-1 and SDN-2 genome-edited plants that are free from exogenous introduced DNA were exempted from Rules 7–11 of the 1989 Rules, which impose GEAC approval requirements and restrictions concerning handling, production, environmental release and specified products and foodstuffs.

This is a conditional exemption from specified provisions, not a declaration that all genome-edited plants are unregulated. Research must remain under containment and Institutional Biosafety Committee oversight until the absence of exogenous introduced DNA is demonstrated. Other applicable laws and requirements continue to matter for the development and release of varieties.

Regulatory distinction: A transgenic crop carrying introduced foreign genetic material and an SDN-1 or SDN-2 genome-edited plant demonstrated to be free from exogenous introduced DNA should not automatically be treated as having the same regulatory pathway.

BioE3 Policy: biotechnology for the economy and environment

On 24 August 2024, the Union Cabinet approved the BioE3 Policy, whose name expands to Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment. Its purpose is to promote high-performance biomanufacturing, innovation and entrepreneurship, including approaches associated with a circular bioeconomy.

The policy identifies 6 broad thematic sectors:

  1. Bio-based chemicals, biopolymers, active pharmaceutical ingredients and enzymes.
  2. Smart proteins and functional foods.
  3. Precision biotherapeutics.
  4. Climate-resilient agriculture.
  5. Carbon capture and utilisation.
  6. Futuristic marine and space research.

The policy also supports development of biomanufacturing facilities, Bio-AI hubs and biofoundries. A biofoundry is a facility intended to support systematic development and evaluation of biological technologies. The BioE3 Policy is a programme for biotechnology development; it is not a replacement for statutory biosafety regulation.

A Government of India parliamentary reply dated 23 July 2026 described BioE3 implementation activities across the identified thematic sectors. Thus, as of the 13 November 2026 content cutoff, BioE3 should be understood as a policy approved in 2024 with implementation activity reported in 2026, rather than merely a future proposal.

Gujarat's biotechnology institutions

Gujarat State Biotechnology Mission

The Gujarat State Biotechnology Mission (GSBTM) operates under the Government of Gujarat's Department of Science and Technology. Its role includes encouraging biotechnology development, entrepreneurship, institutional cooperation and related activity in the state. It is associated with Gandhinagar.

Gujarat Biotechnology Research Centre

The Gujarat Biotechnology Research Centre (GBRC) is an autonomous institution established by the Government of Gujarat's Department of Science and Technology. The official state description records its establishment decision dated 11 August 2017 and commencement on 1 September 2017.

GBRC is based in Gandhinagar. Its activities include biotechnology research and applications relevant to healthcare, agriculture, industry and the environment. These institutions connect biotechnology's national scientific goals with research and development needs in Gujarat.

Connecting the complete subtopic

Industrial, environmental and agricultural biotechnology are connected by the use of biological systems for practical purposes. Enzymes and microorganisms can manufacture useful products; microbial communities can help treat pollution; plant breeding and biological inputs can support agriculture; and synthetic biology can develop new biological functions. These opportunities are accompanied by the need for suitable assessment, safeguards and governance.

Prelims focus

  • The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the 1989 Rules are central to India's genetically engineered organism framework.
  • GEAC means Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee; its renaming from Approval to Appraisal was notified on 16 July 2010 and took effect on 22 July 2010.
  • The 30 March 2022 exemption concerns qualifying SDN-1 and SDN-2 plants free from exogenous introduced DNA and specified Rules 7–11.
  • BioE3 means Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment; it was approved on 24 August 2024.
  • GSBTM and GBRC are Gujarat biotechnology institutions associated with Gandhinagar; GBRC commenced in 2017.
  • Trap: Biosafety addresses accidental harm, while biosecurity additionally addresses deliberate misuse and unauthorised access.

[Sources: Government of India, Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, 1989 Rules and GEAC 'Acts and Rules' and 'About GEAC' pages, consulted 13 November 2026; Department of Biotechnology, 'Guidelines for Safety Assessment of Genome Edited Plants, 2022', section on the 30 March 2022 exemption; Press Information Bureau, Cabinet approval of BioE3 Policy, 24 August 2024; Press Information Bureau, 'Implementation of BioE3 Policy', 23 July 2026; Government of Gujarat, Department of Science and Technology, official pages for Gujarat State Biotechnology Mission and Gujarat Biotechnology Research Centre, consulted 13 November 2026.]
